methods.name: Peer-Median
methods.skip_reason: insufficient narrow peer set in Drones & Autonomous (found 0 same-stage, 0 adjacent-stage, 0 similar-tier; need ≥3)
methods.rationale: 5 same-sector peers exist in Drones & Autonomous, but none of the narrow filters (same-stage / adjacent-stage / similar-valuation-tier) yielded ≥3 datapoints. Falling back to all-sector median would be misleading.

data.narrative:
ACSL, a Japanese drone and autonomous systems company, went public on the Tokyo exchange following its IPO. The valuation analysis confronts a structural constraint: the Drones & Autonomous sector contains only five identifiable peer companies globally, all private. No public comparables exist in this narrow vertical, and the private peer set—Zipline, Joby Aviation, Nuro, Archer Aviation, and Elroy Air—lacks sufficient homogeneity in stage, valuation tier, or business model to support a reliable peer-median multiple.

The peer-median triangulation method is inapplicable here. A meaningful median requires a minimum of three datapoints drawn from same-stage or adjacent-stage companies; the available private peers do not satisfy these filters in sufficient number or consistency. Applying an all-sector median would introduce excessive noise and obscure the specific risk and growth profiles of autonomous systems businesses. Given ACSL's public listing status and the absence of direct public comparables, traditional relative valuation anchoring proves unreliable.

This analysis cannot produce a supported valuation range without additional methodological inputs—such as discounted cash flow modeling, transaction multiples from M&A precedent, or detailed operating metrics—none of which are present in the available data. The core finding is that ACSL's valuation must be informed by factors beyond peer multiples: founder pedigree (Kenzo Nonami), regulatory trajectory in Japan, and fundamental unit economics of its autonomous platform. A full valuation requires these qualitative and operational inputs rather than comparable-company analysis.
